In Volume one of the Arcadian, on page 44, Bob Fabris writes:

"'Memory Dump' program by Gary Moser prints its answers in hexadecimal language.  See what you get for the location 0006.  If it is 61, then your machine is like mine [Bob Fabris], and it is 66, it is like Tom Wood's.  If something else, then we have more variants on the street."

The interesting thing about this comment is that the 3159 ROM (the later, Astrocade ROM) gives you a $61 for memory location $0006.  The PAPER version, as listed in the "Bally On-Board ROM Subroutines," has a $66 in that same memory location.  The ROM print-out has a date of "4/26/78."  The menu's date is "1977."  Could THIS printout be the missing 3164 ROM, or is it ANOTHER variant?  Check it out for yourself, the ROM listing that I'm referring to can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/misc_docs/bally_on-board_rom_subroutines.pdf

Whatever the ROM listing is, it ISN'T the 3159 ROM or the "white" ROM because they both have a $61 at that memory location.

Any ideas?

Adam

> given for all of the machine language programs.  There are several > versions
> of a program called "Color Tunnel."  One of the versions can display up to

Ahh.. had to use modern technology to display, rotate, and zoom up on these tiny scraps of hand-written comments and dissasembly of 25 year old code but.. WOOT!  I got it working!  I'd like more control like having the interrupts work in VBLANK area but hey, can't complain!  It was pretty simple once I looked at a few examples of his interrupt setup code.

Here's what it looks like, swapping out 2 colors in the table.  Part of this is code from Mike White's tutorial and part from the Color Tunnel.  I probably need to pass control for music and other system stuff that I'm blowing off but this is a good start:

ColorBreak1, ColorBreak2 are constants representing which lines I want to interrupt on.
TopLeftColor, TopRightColor, BotLeftColor, BotRightColor are constants for what I want the 2 color registers to be at their
respective places on the screen.

; ----------------------------------------------------------------
; init screen interrupt
InitScreenInt:
DI
IM2
LD A,SIVEC>>8
LD I,A
LD A,SIVEC & $ff
OUT ($0D), A

LD A,ColorBreak1
OUT ($0F), A
EI
RET
; ----------------------------------------------------------------
; Screen interrupt
SIVEC DW ScreenInt
ScreenInt:
PUSH AF

LD A,(CurrentIntLine)
CP ColorBreak1
LD A,ColorBreak2
JR Z,SKP1
LD A,ColorBreak1
SKP1:
LD (CurrentIntLine),A ; keep track of current interrupt scanline
OUT (INLIN),A ; ($0f)
; set colors (one for left side, one for right) based on which part of the screen we are now
LD A,TopLeftColor
JR Z,SKP2
LD A,BotLeftColor
SKP2:
OUT (COL3L),A ; Left Color Register 3
LD A,TopRightColor
JR Z,SKP3
LD A,BotRightColor
SKP3:
OUT (COL3R),A ; Right Color Register 3

POP AF
EI
RET
; ----------------------------------------------------------------

There is a jump table in the on board rom that I showed in my
tutorial under the heading "COLD START". The addresses that this
table jumps to are in the cartridge following the 1st item menu link.
To use them simply tell the Z80 to RESTART. RST 0 starts you over
cold. RST 8 jumps to !2007, RST 10H jumps to !200A, RST 18H jumps to !
200D, RST 20H jumps to !2010, RST 28H jumps to !2013, RST 30H jumps
to !2016, and RST 38H launches you into the on board subroutines.
4008:
Hi all,
Mr Technical here.

On page 76 of the Dave Nutting Manual There is a proof - reading statement that is incorrect. The meaning of "creams alternate set" is:

There is an alternate set of registers inside the Z80 called the prime set.
They are AF' , BC', DE' and HL' (' means prime)
 They are another set just like the standard set EXCEPT you don't work directly with them.
What you CAN do is swap this set with the standard set, making this the active set to work with and preserve the data in the alternate set.
The z8o OP code EXX (D9H or 217d) will swap these registers.
There also is one individual swap to prime, EX AF,AF' (08H or 8d) or [8 dollars for you other ML people]

The saying "cream alternate set" means that the prime set is used by that routine and has not been saved. If you have worked doing an EXX and are expecting the contents to be the same, you're out of luck when you call SYSTEM or SYSUK MENU.

Ken

The "on board" screen interrupt routine is gotten to with a RST 38H
command (see the "on board" subroutine book). In Blue Ram "PLAY" this
routine got called every interrupt. However, it may try to
reinitialize the interrupt to whatever Gunfight and etc. uses. I
never messed with it, but the code for "start up" shows it to be THE
only place for initialization to take place! First off, you only need
to call on it at the bottom of the screen so to get the "vector
animator" to work during vertical retrace. Secondly, you may be
required to re-submit some of your "custom" initalization upon return
from this subroutine. Finally, if you get a lot going on timing
becomes critical. For further help, Lance Squire, or somone else with
more experience than I will be needed to advise you. I wish you the
best of luck with this endevor.

Since I've been typing BASIC programs in for the last few days, I have some hints for those who might never have done it before.

1) Save often.  This should be a no-brainer.  I save my program every fifteen minutes.  Using a computer as a storage device instead of a tape deck makes this MUCH easier.  I can save the program to the computer, use Ballybin and Astrowav 1.4 to clean the program up, and then use verify (the :LIST command) on the saved work.  All of this takes, literally, about two minutes.  Imagine how much time that it can save you if you accidentally hit the RESET button.

2) Check your work over as you go.  When I have filled a screen with BASIC statements, I type CLEAR;LIST <line #> (replace line # with the top-most line statement).  After the lines have printed on the screen I carefully check them against what I'm supposed to type.  I don't always find an error, but I do on occasion.  Finding any entry errors NOW makes testing and playing the program later MUCH easier.

3) Watch your P's and Q's.  I've found that hand-written listings in the newsletters can be difficult to read sometimes.  I've confused "+" with the divide-sign-- even after looking very closely at the statement.  I've also done the typical confusing of the zero with the letter "O" and the number "5" with the letter "S."  You can usually avoid common entry mistakes if you pay attention to what you're typing.  Does typing the word "T00" (with zeros) makes any sence?  Of course not.  Just checking simple things like this can save you from unnecessary preoof-reading later.

4) Make sure to use the WORDS key.  This is an easy one, but could trip-up a beginner.  Also use the WORDS key inside quotes, when possible.  For instance, if inside quotes there is the word "HE WENT TO THE STORE," it is acceptable to use the WORDS key for the word "TO."  In fact, you save yourself a byte (and a keypad stroke!) by doing this.

5)  I've already mentioned this, but verify your program with :LIST.  I've never had any problems that were the computer's fault, but I did have one problem that was avoided because of an error that I made with ballybin.  The :LIST command caught this error and saved me some possible lost program statements.

6) Use different fingers to type on the keypad.  I have to switch between using my index finger and my middle finger when I'm typing on the keypad.  If you don't do this, then you're going to get an awfully sore finger.

7) Test your Program.  Just because you've checked your program carefully as your typed it doesn't mean that there aren't any errors.  I've yet to type in a program longer than several lines that doesn't have a simple error (that I catch while typing).  And EVERY program I've ever typed-in from any magazine always has some errors that I've introduced into it.  The moral here is to run your program through its paces.  Try all of the different possiblities.  Do what you don't expect the program is capable of.  TRY to get the program to crash-- then note the problem down if it DOES crash.

These are just some simple hints that I'm writing while I wait for my index finger and middle finger to recover a bit.  I bet that the newsletters had tips like this, but I don't recall reading them.

I'm sure that some of you may have other general typing hints-- let's hear them!

Adam

I finished typing in and testing "Darts" by Bill Mead.  It works fine in AstroBASIC.  There don't seem to be any compatibility problems at all; the sound works fine.  I emailed a copy off to Paul Thacker for him to try out.  I'll upload the program to the Ballyalleyc.om website when I get a chance.  In the meantime, here are the games instructions (along with archive information):


Astrocade Tape Program Archive Record
-------------------------------------

Program Name:  Darts
Filename:      Darts (1981)(Bill Mead)(2000 Baud)(PD).wav
Released by:   Bill Mead
Appearance:    BASIC Express, 3, no. 1 (April 1981): 3-4.
Notes:         - This program was typed into AstroBASIC on May 10, 2007
                by Adam Trionfo.
              - The program "Darts" is exactly as it appears
                in the BASIC Express newsletter.

Description
-----------

This is a 2000 Baud BASIC program for use with a Bally Astrocade and Astrobasic.

This program allows up to four players to play a very simple game of dart.  Each player uses a different hand controller.


Instructions
------------

"Darts" is a 4-player simulation.  An attempt has been made to simulate realism.  Player may select 1 of 3 different throws.

1. Hard Throw (somewhat erratic).  With this mode, any score is possible, 10-20-30-40, bullseye or complete miss.

2. Moderate Throw (controlled).  Each throw will recieve a score of 10-20-30 or 40.  No possibility of a bullseye of a complete miss.

3. Very Hard Throw - Either a bullseye or a complete miss.

A winning score is 500.  Move joystick left or right to select throw type.  Pull trigger to throw dart.  Upon completion of game, press any key to begin anew.

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):

When I've played darts before there was a heck of a lot more to throwing the dart than just choosing how hard I was going to throw it.  How about aiming the dart?  This game is nothing more than a menu driven game and with some random elements thrown in by the computer.  I don't see any "realism" that the instructions hint at.  If there was a four-player game going on, I could imagine a little bit of stategy.  You might have to decide if you are going to take the fifty-fifty chance at the miss or the bullseye, or if you going to play it safe and take your chances with a sure hit, but for lower points.

This game has simple graphics and sound.  They get the job done; nothing more.  When I say get the job done, that's exactly what I mean.  For, who has ever heard of a SQUARE dart board?  The big drawback to a four-player game is that everyone needs a different controller.


Loading Instructions
--------------------

Plug audio cable into Astrobasic cartridge and headphone jack of computer speakers, then load program from Astrobasic with

:INPUT ;RUN

Press GO.  Then start playing the wav file; the program will start to load.  After the program finishes loading, type RUN and then press GO.

END OF FILE

Some programs are compatible BB to AB, some convert with a few
changes, others cannot run at all regardless what you do. The
differences are in the changes with the sound variables, taping, and
ommitions to allow for the editor and 2000 baud taping.
All programs in The Curser, Basic Express, and Arcadian Vol's 1,2,+3
are BB format unless you come across one in EB or ZGRASS. (see the
software listing to identify formats)
Taping in BB is totally different than AB. In BB the Light Pen
interrupt is used to KEY IN the program one byte (bit serial) at a
time. In other words, when a 300 baud tape ":input"s the tape
simulates the keypad and literally KEYS IN the program just as you
did only faster! There was a scheme (in one of the newsletters) where
someone keyed in a program with a long tape running on ":print" and
had instant backup if the worst occured. All that is fine, untill one
realizes that the backup tape is now over 1/2 hour long! Did someone
say that 3 or 4 minutes was too much? Anyway, if you haven't already
guessed, there was no easy way to load a fixed string, poke machine
code numbers in, or preset the variables and tape all that! So comes
the special taping instructions. In AB the entire memory goes to tape
with :print and will auto-run with machine code and all using
print ";run ";:print %(16384),1887. The command :return only gives an
error message in AB. (In BB it re-initialized the screen interrupt
turning off all tape port activity).
In AB the sound variables were introduced. Indirect sound port access
didn't change (MU=, TV=, or PRINT) so any sound made this way will
work, but not sound the same. See my tutorial on indirect sound port
access. Direct sound port access was changed over to the new
variables. To access the sound ports directly one needs to set bit 7
of the note timer. This turns off ALL sound except direct port
commands >NT=-1. The down side of this was trying to use direct and
indirect access at once to create special effects. Not as easy in AB.
Finally, the $ command *PRINT command, and some machine code routines
won't run in ab at all! The only way to save these at 2000 baud is to
employ the Dave Ibach cartridge swap routine in Arcadian vol IV. Be
sure to catch the correction. You could even tape the program with
the cartridge swap in place saving a key in every time.
Does any of this help?

A couple of programming tips;

Type in the following instead of their counterparts
1 GOTO 5
2BOX X,Y,3,3,3:RETURN

300 GOSUB 300+RND(7)
301 X=10;Y=25;RETURN
301 X=10;Y=5;RETURN
301 X=19;Y=40;RETURN

... etc.
This saves time and bytes, making it run faster.

assuming that a line like this is correct, the result will either have 12 or 0 (zero).
B would be =12 IF B=12 to start with. If B has any number in it besides 12, it will be zero.
To make it easier to see:
B=(B=12). Parens don't always need to be there, but is is good practice to put them there.If you don't know the order of math priority, not having them there can give huge differences!
B=9+2x6-5 will give you 16  9 plus 2x6 minus 5 [(9+12)-5]
if you typed in B=(9+2)x(6-5) your answer would be 11 (9+2=11) x (6-5=1) 11x1=11

Not seeing this program the probability of it being B=B=12 is slim. It is probably B=B+12 or something similar.

Ken

I am using the Editor in AstroBASIC to edit lines.  The directions in the AstroBASIC manual are easy to use, but I was wondering if there might be a feature that is available that isn't listed.  I seem to remember that Ken wrote an article on using the Editor that was published in the Arcadian-- anyone remember which issue the article is in?

Here is what I'm trying to do.  Let's say I have a line that says this:

10 STUFF STUFF OOPS STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF STUFF

I look at the line and I realize that OPPS is supposed to say STUFF.  So I type 10 and then I press PAUSE and correct the word OOPS.  Is there any way to avoid pressing PAUSE until the end of the line (in the above case, another -84- times if each of these letter is one letter and not a WORD)?

I know that if I press GO after the correction, it erases everything after the correction, leaving me with:

10 STUFF STUFF OOPS

If I press HALT after a correct, then the line is unchanged (leaving the error).

I usually just press PAUSE until the end of the line, but with this L&M Software game "WHAT-ZIT" that I'm typing in, each line is LONG.  I'd like to avoid pressing the PAUSE button forty or fifty times after a correction is already made.  The tip of my keypad typing fingers will thank you if you can help me!

Adam

I finished typing in another of Paul Thacker's BASIC program choices.  This time it was L&M Software's game "What-Zit."  The was an error in listing (as I pointed out in a previous message).  Of the three games that I've typed in the last couple of days (two versions of Darts and this game), this is the best game- by far!

When I upload the program to Ballyalley.com, I'll let you know.  Included here is the archive information about the program:

Astrocade Tape Program Archive Record
-------------------------------------

Program Name:  What-Zit
Filename:      What-Zit (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 Baud)(PD).wav
Released by:   L&M Software
Appearance:    BASIC Express, 3, no. 2 (May/June 1981): 22-23.
Notes:         - This program was typed into AstroBASIC on May 11, 2007
                by Adam Trionfo.
              - The program "What-Zit" is exactly as it appears in the
                BASIC Express newsletter, except for one fix.  Without
                this, the program doesn't run correctly.  Line 50 has part
                of the line that says, "B=B=12"  This is incorrect.  The
                statement should be B=B+12

Description
-----------

This is a 2000 Baud BASIC program for use with a Bally Astrocade and Astrobasic.

This game is very-much like the board game Mastermind-- except you don't need a second player, and the entire game can be played with the hand controller.


Instructions
------------

What-Zit is a fun game using your powers of logic, reason, and deduction.  The object is to guess a number the computer picks, using clues given on the screen.  Two difficulty levels are provided.  Level one allows the computer to choose a 4 digit number with no individual digits greater than 5 or less than 1.  Level two again allows the computer to choose a 4 digit number, with no individual digit greater than 9 or less than 1.

To choose a digit squeeze the trigger when the number you want light up.  Should you wish to keep any digits from a previous guess, squeeze your trigger when the blank square lights up.  After you have entered your fourth number the computer will tell you:

1. How many of the digits are in the right place and are correct.
2. How many of the digits are correct but in the wrong place.
3. How many of the digits are wrong.

Just to make it interesting the computer does all of this but does not tell which number is which.  Anytime you want to quit and find out what the computer's number is, squeeze your trigger when you see the "GIVE" sign.  The number of tries you have made is always displayed in the lower right hand corner of the screen.  At the end of your game, should you wish to play another, squeeze your trigger and a new game will begin.

Additional Notes (by Adam Trionfo):

The blank square that lets you keep any digits from the last guess will place a zero into your guess if you use it on your first guess; zero isn't even a choice the computer can choose from.

The computer can pick the same number more than once.  The most that it replicated a number for me was twice, but when I look at the code, it seems that the number can be replicated up to four times.

If you choose to restart again with the trigger, you begin on the same level as you chose when you first began playing the game (one or two).  If you want to start on the other level, then you must quit the game with HALT and then RUN it again.

Since you have to wait for the moving square to get to the number that you want, this game might have been more user-friendly if the hand controller's knob had been used to choose a number instead of waiting for the square with the number that you want to light up.  This game WAS written in 1981; any program that ran at all was user-friendly!

I played this game one both levels, and it would have been impossible (for me) to beat either level without keeping track on paper of which numbers were in the right place per guess.  If you can remember each guess in your head, then you're a MUCH better player than I am!


Loading Instructions
--------------------

Plug audio cable into Astrobasic cartridge and headphone jack of computer speakers, then load program from Astrobasic with

:INPUT ;RUN

Press GO.  Then start playing the wav file; the program will start to load.  After the program finishes loading, type RUN and then press GO.

END OF FILE

When The Bit Fiddlers released the Machine Language Manager cartridge, they released a demo tape that could be purchased with it called "Goldfish Demo" (original price $5).  There was also a machine language listing to go along with it (additional cost of $3) .  The demo was available on tape in three formats: Bally BASIC, AstroBASIC and Machine Language Manager.  There are various ads for this program in the Arcadian newsletter, but the best one is here:

Bit Fiddlers, The. "Goldfish Demo," ARCADIAN 4, no. 7 (May 1982): 74

Here is what the ad says:

    Goldfish Demo!

    Actually, they're neon tetras, but that would make the name too long.  The demo tape is designed to show the power of the Machine Language Manager Cartridge.  It's a relatively short program, but it independently controls the actions of 7 goldfish, a digital clock, and the meowing of a cat.  And it's in 4 colors.
    Animation is smooth and non-blinking.  And GOLDFISH does not require MLM to run.  The program will run with Bally BASIC, Astrovision BASIC, and MLM.
    An interesting sidelight: Once loaded and running, GOLDFISH no longer requires a cartridge in the slot.  You can remove it and the program will keep running until you hit reset.

There is also a short review of the program in the Arcadian in the news section:

Fabris, Bob. "Goldfish," ARCADIAN 4, no. 6 (April 1982): 57

This is what the news bite says:

Goldfish is a program that was developed by Andy Guevara by the use of his Machine Language Monitor [Manager] program.  He displayed it to us at the Faire and it is a cute demonstration piece.  A fish tank appears, a number of fish swim back and forth- continuous motion, no jerks - and a little pussy cat looks longingly.  A clock is included, and every minute, the cat meows.  Andy has the listing for $3., and a tape can be loading into either BASIC (:RUN), or the MLM cartridge, at $5.

Doesn't this sound interesting?  My question is: is there anybody out there that HAS this demonstration program?  Or, even just the ML listing?  I'd love to see it archived!

Adam

After I checked out all of the Arcadian programs that have been archived, I was VERY shocked to see how many programs are still NOT archived that we could "just" type in from the newsletter.  Some of these programs would be hard to archive because they require special equipment (additional RAM, extended BASIC, or parallel ports).  Some of these might be difficult to archive because they are Bally BASIC programs that might not be compatible with Astro BASIC; not many of us that have the patience for that 300-Baud language (plus it can't be digitally archived).

There are MANY programs available on Ballyalley.com for download, but I had no idea that the site was missing so many programs!  Of course, not all the missing progams are games, but MANY of them are either games are graphic programs of some sort.

Is there anyone that is as surprised as I am?!?  Heck, is there anyone that ISN'T surprised?

Adam

I have typed in all of the program names from the Cursor and BASIC Express newsletters.  There are 65 programs, most of which have not been archived.  Figuring out which of these have been archived will take more time than it did with the Arcadian.  The "Cursor / BASIC Express" download section on ballyalley.com only has four programs.  However, from reading through this list, some of these programs are available in other download areas.  I'd say, off hand, that there may be about ten to fifteen others archived.  Still that leave about fifty Cursor programs that have not been archived; that's 80% of the collection.

Except for one program, none of the Cursor programs appear to be written in an extended BASIC, nor do any of them seem to require any unusual hardware; they should each work well with Bally or Astro BASIC.  Quite a few of the early programs probably will only work with Bally BASIC-- but that's better than being in a language that isn't available at all!

While going through the Niagara BUG Bulletin for program listings I found this neat trick, and for most people (I bet) impossible to perform, trick.  This is an excerpt from:

O'Neill, Kevin. "Cartridge Swapping," Niagara BUG Bulletin 2, no. 2 (January [?] 1984): 9


The menu sequence for the selection of game parameters in the cartridge games is the perfect opportunity to swap carts.  The following are little "tricks" that I've discovered that get pretty interesting results.

Play Incredible Wizard and write down your score.  Now, without resetting, put in the Blast Droids cart [which all Astrocade user have, right!?!].  From the menu, pick Blast Droids, Training Sector.  Swap to Incredible Wizard.  Now choose 2 players, and the rest of the options as requested, and needed.  Now, with the game begins you should be starting with the score as your last left the game, but with a full supply of men!  Hacking does have its rewards, folks!


If anyone tries this, let me know your results.  This brings 2600 "Frying" to a whole new level-- right, Russ?

Adam

in multiple formats, but only archived in some (Flying Ace in 2000
baud but no working 300 baud version).  And some will be finished
(Esoterica programs, check).

I'm not sure how close to completion we can get on this, but I hope we
do as much as we can.  This system is an interesting case for
archiving since the BASIC cart and tape interface made it a computer
of sorts, so many independent developers sprung up.  I'd say we might
still run into missing programs from the more important developers,
like Bit Fiddlers and L&M.  I doubt we'll ever find some of the more
obscure ones.  Some are known only from small ads in the Arcadian.  I
wouldn't be shocked if no one bought a few of those programs.

As for type-in programs, I certainly encourage Adam to type in
anything he's interested in.  :-)  Looking though the unarchived list,
here's another suggestion:  Strategic Air Command by Bob Weber and
George Moses, Arcadian volume 6, number nine, page 84.  This was
originally published by Bob Weber in Arcadian volume 3, issue 7, page
76, in Bally BASIC format, then later modified George Moses as an
Astro-BASIC program.  Mike White's list notes that the modified
listing is missing the last few lines, so hopefully these will plug in
correctly from the original.

Paul

>>
The [programs] in the newsletters at least can be typed in (though it would be a huge task to do them all--I was hoping Bob Colbert would fix up Ballybin v2 so it could make the process easier).
>>

After typing in about ten programs over the last week or so, I've come to the conclusion that being able to type in the programs on the computer would only be a little bit faster, but not by too much.  That might seem like a crazy statement, given that there are only twenty-four keys to work with on the Astrocade compared to a 101-key or 104-key keyboard on a PC, but I can list my reasons:

1) Many of the programs use the WORDS, and they only require two keystrokes on an Astrocade.  It's pretty amazing how much of the programs are just made up of WORDS.

2) The parts of the programs that are not made up by words are very much made up of numbers.  Even on the Astrocade they only require one keystroke.

3) Even "long" programs on the Astrocade are short, just 1.8K at the most.  The largest program that Ive typed in, a full page, took about two hours.  It wasnt finished in two hours though, because I had to test it.

4) There are several characters on the Astrocade keypad that are not available in ASCII.  Ballybin on the PC has to have a way for you to type them in, and it isn't pretty.  For example, in AstroBASIC there is a divide sign and a multiply sign (among quite a few other characters) that you have to type in long strings on the PC in order to get the equivalent.  I see no way to avoid this.  Its actually quite a bit faster to just use the Astrocade keypad in this situation.

5) After typing in about two or three regular length programs you get pretty well acquainted to the Astrocade keypad.  Just like when you learn to type on a regular keyboard, when you go from using two fingers to ten fingers, you learn to use two fingers on the Astrocade's keypad.  For me, I press the COLOR and WORDS key with the "extra" finger.  It might not seem like a big step, but you just about doubled your typing speed on the Astrocade.

6) The biggest obstacle when typing in a program is to make sure that you type it in EXACTLY as it is listed.  No matter how well you type on the PC, you're bound to make errors when typing in the BASIC program listing.  In fact, I believe that over-confidence in knowing how to type on the PC could make you make more errors.

7) One of the most time consuming parts of typing in a program listing isn't the typing in of the program, but the TESTING of the program to make sure that it works correctly.  This can only be done on the Astrocade (since the emulator doesn't support tape loading).  To fix these errors, you're going to have to know how to use BASIC to some limited extent (at least).  BASIC will give you the equivalent of a "syntax error" and will highlight the error with a question mark, but the error isn't always where the question mark is placed.  You'll have to know how to list a program a few lines at a time (working within the tight space of the 26-column screen), and you'll have to use the AstroBASIC editor.

Im NOT saying that we dont need a foolproof method of typing BASIC programs on the PC (Ballybin isnt quite there yet).  Its just that using a PC wont be as easy as I think people expect it to be.  If the MESS emulator supported the full keyboard and tape emulation, then THAT would be the ideal way to type in a BASIC program!

Adam

4083:
Well, I think you're just about right, but there is
some level of strategy to the game.  You and the enemy
both have a limited number or missiles, which are
fired five at a time in random positions.  So,
depending on how successful your first defense is, you
might or might not decide to fire your missiles again
in that round, and risk running out later.  Some of
the population will inevitably be sacrificed, but you
have to try and save as many as you can.  It seems to
be pretty hard to win, and I gave up after a little
while since it's really not all that fun.

Paul

It turns out that these missiles can be controlled... to some extent.  While I still can't figure-out what the knob is supposed to do (and neither Mike White or I can find any reference to it in the code), it turns out that pushing left or right on the hand controller will move ALL of the missiles in the direction that is pushed.  This isn't really that helpful because if you have some missiles that are going to hit the descending missiles, then you will make those missles miss their target.

The sound is sort of messed up too.  There is no explosion when the missiles hit the city (maybe there isn't supposed to be a sound?).

>>
It seems to be pretty hard to win
>>

IS there a way to beat the game?  I guess that if you don't lose over 100,000 of your population and the enemy has no missiles left, then you win.   Loosing 99,000 of your population and still winning isn't much of a win though...

I gave up after a little while since it's really not all that fun.
>>

Nope.  Not too fun at all!  The game is slow-- which isn't unusual for a BASIC game, but the slowness of the game gets in the way of the "fun-ness" of the game.  I will give the game some points for making a pretty convincing cityscape; I like the way that it looks.

4113:
Extended memory schemes always started at !6000 so as to
allow "readressing" for cartridge testing from tape! Blue Ram's
memory went from !6000 to !707F, then extended on to !A07F for the
16K version, and to !E07F in the 32K version. Viper started at !6000
and went to !9FFF for a Viper 1 and then went on to !DFFF in the
Viper 5! I'm not sure if (or how many) Viper 5's were built. All
these systems had the feature of being able to play game cartridges
WITHOUT the cartridge by keeping a software copy of such on a
cassette tape. To play the game, simply load the tape to !6000,
switch your system from 6K RAM mode to 2K ROM mode, and hit RESET!

The 64K Ram Board from R&L didn't have this feature however.
Henseforth, it accesses !5000 to !FFFF and has slots to replace
everything below !5000 as well!

The only other memory expansion idea that excesses !5000 is the
schematic that I circulated some time back. Although Astro Basic DOES
have access to this area, no software that I know (so far) uses it.

4118:
Adam;

The Abbreviations such as Bo. for BOX Etc. appeared only with Hot Rod
Basic, Vipersoft Basic, And Blue Ram Basic (extended memory systems
only), and was kept in memory as 3 bytes each, except some of the
single character abbreviations such as D. for DATA which used 2
bytes. Henseforth, the "keywords" were the most efficent WHEN THEY
COULD BE USED! Some commands such as OP or PLAY had to be abbreviated
or spelled out and they took as many bytes as the number of
characters that appears on the screen!
Using the extended memory scheme may be compatible as the "keyword"
code didn't change between basics. The extra "keywords" that appear
in the extended systems have a code following the old Bally Basic
code (from 120 to 127 decimal). However, full keyboard entry was
never possible with Astro Basic, and there is no editor in old BB. So
an emulator that "does it all" may not be as easy as it sounds since
the keypad on the arcade didn't allow for the extra words in BRB
either!

The way that it is supposed to work, is that you load a program, wait until the LED glows red, and then turn the volume a little above that.  In practice though, I've noticed that you have to sometimes go WAY above it.  I've noticed that it really depends on the quality of the equipment that you are using: speakers, CD player, computer or sound card.  I've even noticed that different AstroBASIC cartridges will require different levels when using an identical setup.  Once you start to see SOMETHING on the screen (even garbage) when loading from "tape," that's GOOD.  When you finally see stuff on the screen, you usually just have to give it a little more volume and then you are set; the program should load fine.

Tony; (or anyone that can answer this)

Do you know the exact order that signals occur going out the 50 pin
connector? (For a memory read or write cycle)

The ram doc's that they have on line today give a warning about trying
to read from two addresses at the same time. If dissimilar data tries
to appear on the "IO" buss, the bits that are dissimilar effectivly
cause a short between logic 1 "5v" and 0 "0v". To insure this doesn't
happen and destroy the ram, it is recommended that the (negative)
output enable be kept high (off) untill a read is called for. The
arcade has a (negative) read enable signal going out the 50 pin
connector, but my Blue Ram schematic doesn't make use of it. However,
the schematic for the 64K Ram Board does! I would like to be sure that
the system enable, cassette enable, and buzzoff circuits have enough
time to respond to a memory expansion read or write request BEFORE the
external ram STARTS to read. I can change where these lines tie into if
necessary.

That is my fade-in/fade-out color version of "The Game of LIFE" and I

the core code by hand in machine code looking up the octal codes on a
card.

I used Hot-Rod Bally Basic (with keyboard) and wrote the routine in
extended
memory on my 64K bare-board kit from R&L (who conveniently lived near me
and
Midway Manufacturing - where I worked during the Pac-Man craze of the
80's)
and I also had an EEPROM burner from them so I could save off changes to
it.

It only did one generation to whatever was on the screen and then redrew
it
but that worked well enough that I was able to get some time (and much
help)
on R&L's cp/m machine and write it in assembly language then
cross-assemble.


The finished version only kept track (at the bottom of the screen) of if
a
pixel needed to change and then x-or'd it while the screen was
blue-on-black
in between ramping colors to simulate the cells being born and dying.
There
was a little flicker in the population counter that I wasn't able to
solve.

Program counters and variables were hidden on the side using basic's
trick.

The playfield was only 64 x 128 but it wrapped around instead of just
ending
to better simulate an infinite space, which made the patterns on page 4
work!

(Those non-descending descenders reminds me I never got that printer
back!!)

Each generation took about two seconds since each cell always did 8
BITTSTs
and I didn't like the uneven speed that using a bounding box would
create.
I looked at Jay Fenton's code and could not make any sense out of it at
all!

Besides the slow speed, I was disappointed that some working code that I
had
temporarily commented out (to keep it all under 2K) never got put back
in:
If you pause (by hitting any key) you can move the group to the right &
down
but not left or up! You had to slide it all the way around to get it
over!

Also, I didn't get a chance to change the working title to something
better
like "Conway's LIFE" before taking them to a Michigan AstroBugs
gettogether,
and I worried that someone would order one from their newsletter
expecting
a clone of a certain Milton Bradley board game that shared the same
name...

In the files section is a hand-drawn schematic of the BalCheck hardware.
It should be a fax-sized grayscale GIF but Yahoo has a habit of
shrinking things down. Does anyone use the beta Rich-text editor on
here? I noticed that italicized song names came out in bold instead!

anyone? Can everyone see the different fonts I use, or should I cut it
out?

Back to the BalCheck - the display latch port on page 27 of the
home_video_burn-in_tester_with_source.pdf circuit is not fully decoded;
it will react to OUT(240) thru (255)! The actual hardware used the same
chip count, with the latches being custom 9374 PALs (or was that PLAs?)
but I neglected to identify the segments that they drove or the pin
numbers on the LEDs. I think the ground on pin 5 defeated the
leading-zero suppression as I'm sure it displayed "00" instead of
blanks.

One strange thing is that pin 21 of the 2716 is driven by A13, isn't
that supposed to be Vpp? Anyways, it worked. The note about "may not
work with ..." was because I had versions with changed checksums that it
was looking for to match the newer system ROMs - even one to work in the
Professor Pac-Man arcade game I had briefly.

send it, as the file area on here looks like it was gutted. Also there
is a 2000 baud tape cassette interface that might be a little messy, but

4145:
Richard;

Are these Beatle Music programs of yours on cassette tapes or roms? I
have a working Arcade and a hommade "rom reader" cartridge similar to
the one that Rusty and Dale had back in 1983. I call it "BUBBA II" as
in the Arcadian Vol. 4 where one called "BUBBA" was for sale, but
only had a 24 pin ZIF! Mine (and Rusty's) have a 28 pin socket. It's
wired to accept the "27 series" EPROMS from the 2732 through the
27512. In other words, I can read in programs on 2000 baud tapes, or
any 27 series EPROMS. Then copy it off onto casette tape, or burn
each song on it's own EPROM, or put all 8 in one large EPROM and have
it selectable from switches as I said earlier.

"My UPS store became a ShipItHere and the cheapest rate was "Postal Service". "USPS?", I asked, and again was told "Postal Service" and that it would be $13.72! I should have gone to the real US Post Office but I was on foot today. Whatever was in the box I re-used only ran $1.84 postage - so did I get ripped off or is that a fair price?"

I started mailing out a lot of stuff (ebay sales etc.) a few months ago and learned some things about shipping.  First thing I learned is to avoid the "ship it now" type of places as they always jack up the price no matter what shipping service is used.  USPS is the cheapest and convienient still (UPS will not send to a PO box and for anything overseas they have no "slower" option so things tend to be VERY expensive).  Now USPS raised their rates about a month ago but they are still the best option.  I really reccomend using Priority Mail from them for a couple reasons.  First, they will supply the box for free (you can have them mail you a bunch or you can just ask them at the Post Office).  Second, stuff that I have not sent Priority Mail recently has often turned up late and/or damaged.  The minimum cost for a Priority Mail ship right now is $5.60 and that goes up to a pound in weight.

Prices are a lot higher for shipping these days but still can be kept reasonable by going to the good ole Post Office.

Mike G

--- In ballyalley@yahoogroups.com, "Mike White" <mike@...> wrote:
>
> Tony; (or anyone that can answer this)
>
> Do you know the exact order that signals occur going out the 50 pin
> connector? (For a memory read or write cycle)
>
> The ram doc's that they have on line today give a warning about trying
> to read from two addresses at the same time. If dissimilar data tries
> to appear on the "IO" buss, the bits that are dissimilar effectivly
> cause a short between logic 1 "5v" and 0 "0v". To insure this doesn't
> happen and destroy the ram, it is recommended that the (negative)
> output enable be kept high (off) untill a read is called for. The
> arcade has a (negative) read enable signal going out the 50 pin
> connector, but my Blue Ram schematic doesn't make use of it. However,
> the schematic for the 64K Ram Board does! I would like to be sure that
> the system enable, cassette enable, and buzzoff circuits have enough
> time to respond to a memory expansion read or write request BEFORE the
> external ram STARTS to read. I can change where these lines tie into if
> necessary.
>

Mike;

Sorry I haven't responded with a decent answer before now.  Shortly
after your original posting, I left the country on a business trip and
only got back a few days ago.  I've not had access to a BPA schematic
during that time.  I think the only thing you need to worry about is
to hold of the OE# on your RAM until all the gating has a chance to
settle down.  If you look at the BPA schematic, note the 3-input NAND
gate controlling pin 9 of U10.  The NAND gate is U13 pin 12.  This pin
will go to logical 1 any time a read occurs from the Casette or System
ROMS, or any time BUZOFF# is asserted.  If you invert this signal and
connect it to the OE# of your RAM, you should be okay.

Cheers,

Tony Miller

Wow, all quiet on the Bally front.  I've been periodically scanning
stuff that Mike White sent me along with items from my own collection,
and have made a few discoveries.  We all know that there are Bally and
Astrovision versions of instructions, the Bally versions being the
small cards and the the Astrovision versions being the large booklets.
 As it turns out, there are more variations that just this.
Sometimes, Bally instructions for the same game will have different
pictures on the front--I've seen this with Tornado Baseball and
Dodgem, for example. With the Astrovision releases, sometimes the box
and instruction booklet will say Bally, and sometimes it will say
Astrocade.  In the case of the Astrocade instruction booklets, they
fold out instead of being stapled and have a more stylized font.  Some
games were released in both Bally and Astrocade versions, including
Galactic Invasion and...Adam's going to love this...AstroBASIC.  Yes,
just like Bally BASIC, there's a second version of the AstroBASIC
instructions with minor revisions.

There are a lot of instructions available now, though with all these
variations popping up it will be hard to say when the collection is
truly complete.  Adam, have you made any progress with the remaining
scans and programs I uploaded awhile ago?  Fair warning--the next
upload's going to be HUGE.  The programs you typed in haven't made it
on-line yet, either.  I've been working on a few programs from Mike,
so we can look forward to some good program additions along with the
scans.  I finally got Quadra for AstroBASIC working.  Ballybin tends
to choke on recordings with many loads, and Quadra had so many that I
eventually split it up, processed them separately, then pasted them
back together.  But, I got a good recording in the end.  I'm glad to
try the 2000 baud version of this.  I played the 300 baud version
earlier and since you had to reload after each round, the loading
times were excrutiating.  Now, it's merely annoying.  :-)

Paul

4194:
>I have been able to test Michael Garber's new cartridge game on the
> emulator, but he doesn't want the game talked about.  So I will say > nothing
> in particular about it except that it is well done and that the graphics > are
> smooth.

It's ok to talk about the game now.  I was planning to release it as a surprise for the 2007 CGE but got distracted by
other things to actually get the cartridges made and became ill while the actual event was in town so that didn't get
going.  The rom I sent you is more or less the final version.  I had 1 or 2 things I was thinking to add to it but there
were only a couple hundred bytes left (out of 8k) but I probably wont bother trying to do them at this point.  I am \
thinking of getting the thing put together in a cart with Mike White's help and selling a limited run (perhaps only 10
or 20), followed by a generic one that could be made on demand by Mike.  I had not planned to release the rom
but if most Bally enthusiasts do not have an actual Bally to play the game on, I may change my mind about that.  I still
have to get a decent label made for it and a simple instruction manual.

> There are two things in this game that really strike me.
>
> 1) The number of colors.  This game has more colors during GAMEPLAY than > any
> other Astrocade game.  Easy.
>
> 2) Number of moving objects on the screen that move about.  They move VERY
> smoothly.

I did spend some time trying to get a lot of color into the game and was pleased with the end result.  Not much
was wasted here as every scan line was taken into account when switching between colors when possible.  Many
of the routines I wrote were optimized for speed and, although I haven't seen it running on the actual hardware yet,
if the emulation is accurate at all.. it should be one of the fastest running games on the system.

> Once the game is released on cartridge, could the source code (with
> explanations) be put on the Internet?

I don't want to release the entire source code but I would have no problem putting up parts of it with explinations.
Without the help I got from the guys in this group and your extensive documentations on Bally Alley, this game
would never have even been started.  I'd love to help others by sharing what I've learned if I can.

>  Does the game use the built-in ROM
> sub-routines for the graphics or does it use its own routines?  I wonder > if
> Mike could even possibly write a tutorial about getting smooth graphics
> moving around the screen.

It uses the built-in ROM routines for most of the drawing.  For erasing and doing collision vs the background
I wrote some optimized routines built for speed (at the expense of code space).  At one point I used the RECTAN
routine to erase the "fireballs" but it would slow down when I got multiple fireballs on-screen at once and detracted
from the gameplay.  The collision vs the background is actually quite robust and the direction the fireballs bounce off
stuff is based on the shape of what they collide with.

I'm glad you were able to get a chance to check it out.  If it runs smoothly on the hardware OK I'll get these
carts made up and a web page with a detailed description of the game with screen shots in the next month or so.
I plan to make some other games in the future if this gets recieved ok =) The game was finished at the end of May,
seems like a long time ago.

Mike G.

Game is called War (or Bally War), based heavily on the coin-op game from Atari called Warlords.  It's a game for 1-4 players where you defend your castle vs 3 other warlords in a survival match. A player is destroyed if a fireball makes it's way into the inner core of his or her castle.  Additional fireballs are thrown into the mix as time goes on and play continues until only 1 player is left alive. 4208:
Well, if everybody is going to comment on what they were doing during
the last months, maybe I can show something too.

I wasn't going to release this to public, as I failed in my main
objective with it ( to get Astrocade BASICs running) and as it is a
piece of very poorly written code, but I tried to make an Astrocade
Emulator, using Blitz3D.

What can I comment about it:

Z80: The Z80 instruction set has many bugs and isn't fully
implemented yet. I used in it the Z80 emulation code I designed for
an MSX emulator (this one is in a much more advanced state, with many
games fully playable). As I said before, the code used in it is very
badly written (I use result dumps for many Z80 instructions that I
was't able to figure out the correct flag behavior).

Video: Euch! I got pallete values from an HTML file I found at Bally
Alley, and I don't really know how they were generated (the formulas
used to convert chrominance and luminance to RGB). There are many
Magic Memory functions missing , the other ones are probably all
wrong :)

Sound: Well, no sound by now...

Input: Only PC keyboard is supported by now (for the console keypad
and joystick 1)


As I said, my objective when I started it was to get Basic running,
so I could try to implement tape reading support. Unfortunately, all
I get from the Basic cartdriges is a black screen, and as the
debugging tools I made until now aren't really useful to find out
what is wrong, the project is stalled, until I make further
enhancements to the emulation engine (through its shared code with
the MSX emulator).

If there is somebody out there who has enough courage to try it out,
here it is:

http://eggerland.googlepages.com/Bally.rar

Basic usage instructions:

Unpack all files to a folder. Open a command prompt, change current
directory to the folder containing the .exe file and type ballyemul
to get it running without a cartdrige. To run it using a cartdrige (I
included TESTS.BIN, the only one making something usable by now) type
ballyemul gamename.bin (replace gamename with the desired game file
name, and dont forget to add the file extension).

The keyboard layout is as follows:

Cursor keys - match the equivalent ones for joystick 1

Space - fire button for joystick 1

123456
QWERTY
ASDFGH
ZXCVBN

These keys match the Astrocade keypad port by port, as in page 102 of
nutting manual (Z is Astrocade's CE, X is 1, Y is 4, and so on).

[Esc] - Quits the emulator.

The emulator will run at fullscreen, but the output is displayed in
the upper left corner,as the rest of the screen is used for debugging
(when a non implemented instruction is found, it displays Z80
register information, among other things).

That's it! Although it is a lame emulator, you have to keep in mind
some aspects: I already said I'm a bad programmer, and I never saw a
real Astrocade. In fact, the first time I heard about it was at the 
beginning of March, when I registered to this list, and all
development was made since then (and I just spent some spare time in
it). I got all the information to make it from documentation at Bally
Alley.

Sorry about the poor English, and the long message!


Ronaldo Goulart

4248:
I added the program "The Collatz Conjecture."  This a mathmatical demonstration.  Check this program out, as it's pretty neat to watch the Astrocade go through the math.

From the game loading screen:

About 30 years ago [1937] a professor named Collatz created this thought provoker. Start with any whole number.  If it is odd, triple it +1. If it is even, take half.  Repeat. The final result will always be one. Why is that?  After all, the odd number is tripled + 1. This more than compensates for the halves???

Sample program run:

THE COLLATZ CONJECTURE

START WITH ANY WHOLE  NUM-
BER.  IF IT IS ODD, TRIPLE
IT +1. IF IT IS EVEN, TAKE
HALF.  REPEAT.  THE  FINAL
RESULT WILL ALWAYS BE ONE.
I WILL COMPUTE FOR YOU.

INPUT A NUMBER

[The program now will run for a while, printing the
results on screen until the answer is one, then it
will ask for another number.]

For more information about this mathmatical idea, check out the Internet:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collatz_conjecture

To download "The Collatz Conjecture:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Collatz%20Conjecture,%20The%20(Jim%20Dunson).zip

Enjoy!
